candidate.title: Bart Ehrman vs James White — Does the Bible Misquote Jesus? (2009)
candidate.label: Does the Bible Misquote Jesus?
candidate.sourceNote: This assessment covers both formal openings, rebuttals, cross-examinations and closing statements, approximately 0:23–2:28:59. Audience Q&A, logistical interjections and the outro are excluded and supply no credit, penalty or inference of a failure to reply. Both speakers accept textual variants: Ehrman argues that important wording changed and some originals remain uncertain; White defends reliable recovery and continuity of the New Testament’s message. Each is assessed on the position actually defended. Public automatic captions were supplemented by five targeted automated audio checks; these were not direct human listening. The complete public caption record was retained for scope and attribution checks. Exact quotations preserve caption wording; argument summaries and critiques are condensed assessments, and manuscript dates, counts and scholarly claims are evaluated as presented in the debate. One long automated audio check ended before its clip ended; no independent audio verification is claimed beyond the text actually returned.
candidate.scoringNote: Scores are AI-generated estimates of argumentative performance, rather than judgments about worldview truth; the separate AI Contribution does not affect these scores.
candidate.summary: Ehrman narrowly prevailed by proving consequential local misattributions, while White strongly defended recoverable textual and theological continuity.

pro.context: Ehrman closes by focusing on the manuscripts Christians actually used, arguing that scribal mistakes in transmitted words of Jesus make historical Bibles locally misattribute wording.

con.context: White closes by distinguishing copying differences from false quotation, grounding his denial in recoverable apostolic teaching and continuity of Jesus’s message across the manuscript tradition.

pro.words: Successive hand copies inherited earlier mistakes, introduced additional ones, and eventually lost the exemplars needed to identify every original word.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman supplies a concrete cumulative mechanism in which inherited alterations, fresh copying errors, attempted corrections, and disappearing exemplars jointly explain why mere survival does not authenticate every word. Principal limitation: the illustrative chain is deliberately simplified and does not yet incorporate comparison among independently circulating witnesses, so it establishes vulnerability rather than the probable corruption of any particular passage; the analysis therefore remains probabilistic until independent genealogical relationships and identifiable consequential readings connect this vulnerability to the surviving record. Live burden: he must connect this possible failure process to identifiable readings while allowing that cross-comparison can expose many errors. Locked score: 83/100 because the causal sequence is lucid, relevant, and historically intelligible, yet its linear presentation incompletely represents the distributed evidence White later emphasizes.

con.words: A larger manuscript population mechanically produces more recorded variants while also supplying more comparisons, so the raw variant total cannot measure textual unreliability by itself.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White correctly reframes the intimidating aggregate by explaining that additional manuscripts simultaneously multiply detectable differences and expand the comparative evidence available for recovering earlier readings. Principal limitation: abundance alone does not determine whether a consequential reading is recoverable, and the presentation risks moving too quickly from a denominator correction to confidence about particular disputed locations; consequently the denominator clarification should govern rhetoric about scale without functioning as a shortcut around the individual evidential disputes. Live burden: he must classify the variants and demonstrate how distribution, age, and genealogy resolve meaningful alternatives rather than merely increasing observations. Locked score: 87/100 because the quantitative correction directly neutralizes a misleading raw comparison, while still requiring passage-level analysis before it can establish reliable reconstruction.

pro.words: The beloved woman-taken-in-adultery narrative appears in many Bibles although manuscript evidence presented in the debate indicates that it was not original to John.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman anchors the abstract problem in a familiar, substantial Jesus narrative and ties its later insertion to absence from the oldest authorities rather than relying on the emotional force of its popularity. Principal limitation: the selected passage compresses the underlying manuscript case into an appeal to the oldest authorities and an assurance that numerous reasons support the conclusion, without presenting those reasons in detail; absence of comparison limits auditability even though White does not contest the conclusion. Live burden: if the conclusion is challenged, he must unpack the textual evidence; for this debate, he need only establish that Bibles transmitted a sizeable nonoriginal Jesus narrative. Locked score: 91/100 because the example is memorable, evidentially focused, and directly relevant, with unusually strong textual confidence despite compressed supporting detail.

con.words: White separates meaningless spelling differences and implausible readings from variants that both affect meaning and could be original, sharply narrowing the genuinely disputed set.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White replaces the undifferentiated variant total with an analytically useful taxonomy covering untranslatable differences, nonviable readings, ordinary mistakes, harmonizations, and purposeful alterations. Principal limitation: the numerical estimate for meaningful viable variants depends substantially on reported scholarly calculation, and the percentage framing compresses how variant units relate to total textual words; the estimate’s authority dependence especially matters because classification judgments determine which disagreements enter the consequential remainder under discussion. Live burden: he must adjudicate the consequential remainder rather than suggest that its smaller size automatically resolves its interpretive significance. Locked score: 88/100 because the classification is precise, responsive, and candid about a residual problem, although its empirical estimate receives less independent demonstration than its conceptual distinctions.

pro.words: The final twelve verses of Mark were added by scribes, yet they contain memorable resurrection appearances, missionary commands, and practices attributed to Jesus.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman identifies a lengthy disputed ending and specifies recognizable content that entered the received narrative, making the practical consequence of textual addition unusually concrete. Principal limitation: the selected presentation largely reports the conclusion, invokes the oldest and best manuscripts, and gestures toward longstanding scholarly reasons without displaying the complete evidence behind the textual judgment; the missing presentation chiefly affects evidential transparency rather than relevance to the exact attribution question. Live burden: if White disputed the addition, Ehrman would need to provide those reasons; within this exchange, its uncontested textual status already supports the narrower attribution claim. Locked score: 91/100 because the substantial, familiar example bears directly on words assigned to Jesus, although its evidential foundation is summarized rather than demonstrated comprehensively.

con.words: Even when disputed passages supplied familiar proof texts, White argues that essential Christian beliefs generally retain support in other, textually undisputed passages.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White answers the doctrinal implication without denying the disputed passages, using Ehrman’s published qualification to distinguish loss of one proof text from loss of the belief it supported. Principal limitation: redundancy of doctrine cannot establish the original wording at the challenged location and therefore does not alone answer whether a Bible there attributes nonoriginal language to Jesus; the argument succeeds most completely against theological-collapse rhetoric, while the debate’s wording question continues to demand attention to individual attributions. Live burden: he must justify why continuity of essential belief is the appropriate measure of misquotation rather than an important but narrower theological safeguard. Locked score: 90/100 because the reply is accurate, strategically concessive, and strongly supported, while leaving the motion’s local attribution problem substantially intact.

pro.words: Variants affecting Jesus’s prayer for forgiveness and his claimed knowledge of the end illustrate uncertainty about whether particular sayings were originally present.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman moves from long additions to compact sayings whose presence or absence changes what a Gospel explicitly places on Jesus’s lips, bringing the motion into exact verbal focus. Principal limitation: the brief examples identify consequential uncertainty but give little manuscript detail about the competing witnesses or the comparative grounds for choosing either reading; the compact treatment therefore leaves the audience dependent on Ehrman’s reported textual assessment at both locations. Live burden: if he claims a determinate secondary reading, he must supply that missing comparison; the more limited conclusion that original wording remains disputed follows without proving which alternative is false. Locked score: 87/100 because the examples are highly relevant and interpretively meaningful, though their compressed evidential presentation supports scoped uncertainty more strongly than a final textual verdict.

pro.words: Ehrman challenges White’s early-manuscript numbers by requesting the dozen witnesses and disputing their dating, while correcting his own mistaken repetition of 200 to 120.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman tests a concrete empirical premise by demanding enumeration and dating grounds, exposing that White cannot supply the promised complete list during the exchange. Principal limitation: uncertainty about several dates does not erase the broader existence of early witnesses, and failure to reproduce a list extemporaneously does not refute its underlying source; the exchange consequently lowers confidence in the precision of White’s numerical presentation without establishing an alternative complete chronology. Live burden: Ehrman must establish how much the corrected chronology weakens independent reconstruction rather than treating incomplete documentation as decisive disproof. Locked score: 89/100 because the cross-examination is precise, appropriately self-correcting, and evidentially productive, although it leaves the actual witness count unresolved within the debate.

con.words: Early witnesses from multiple intersecting transmission lines, White argues, prevent centralized rewriting and provide geographically distributed comparisons for reconstructing earlier text.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White offers a preservation mechanism rather than bare reassurance: uncontrolled, intersecting circulation makes coordinated alteration harder and permits agreements across streams to carry evidential weight. Principal limitation: the cited early counts are incompletely documented and later challenged, while multiplicity after branching cannot by itself verify the wording of a shared pre-branch ancestor; the distinction between resistance to coordinated revision and positive recovery of autograph wording is indispensable for evaluating the preservation claim. Live burden: he must demonstrate genuine independence, geographic dispersion, and sufficiently early divergence for the selected readings. Locked score: 82/100 because the distributed-transmission inference materially advances reconstruction, but its empirical premises and its reach across the earliest unobserved interval remain insufficiently established.

pro.words: Agreement between P75 and Vaticanus demonstrates continuity within a related stream, Ehrman argues, but cannot by itself represent every early line or reach the autograph.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman grants that P75 and Vaticanus demonstrate continuity within a related Alexandrian stream, then precisely questions what that pair can establish about earlier copying and the wider tradition. Principal limitation: restricting one pair’s reach does not assess the cumulative force of White’s other claimed transmission lines, and the selected exchange does not supply a broader comparative sample; that limitation concerns evidential coverage, not a defect in the concession he grants to the pair. Live burden: if Ehrman wants to weaken the network argument rather than this illustration alone, he must extend the same genealogical analysis across genuinely independent witnesses. Locked score: 90/100 because the challenge accurately limits the inference from an important pair while preserving what their agreement does show, with its remaining weakness confined to wider representativeness.

con.words: Because readings persist throughout the large manuscript tradition, White contends that textual criticism usually chooses among surviving alternatives instead of inventing an absent original.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White states a testable preservation thesis: the same tenacity that conserves scribal mistakes should also conserve original readings somewhere within the collective tradition. Principal limitation: persistence after a reading enters circulation does not logically guarantee survival from the autograph, especially if all extant branches descend from an already altered ancestor; a preservation tendency observed in the extant tradition cannot automatically certify the unavailable interval before those witnesses begin. Live burden: he must support universal availability at consequential variants and address acknowledged occasions when critics consider conjectural emendation. Locked score: 81/100 because tenacity plausibly explains why abundant alternatives assist recovery, but the argument overextends a strong general tendency into assurance about the earliest inaccessible stage.

pro.words: Ehrman distinguishes possibility from probability and offers a plausible conjectural emendation to show that critics may judge every surviving reading secondary, without claiming the conjecture is proved.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman directly identifies the modal overreach in White’s challenge, conceding that an extant reading could be original while denying that mere possibility establishes its probability. Principal limitation: his Enoch proposal for First Peter is presented as a plausible scholarly conjecture rather than a demonstrated instance where every surviving reading is secondary; the example functions best as evidence against necessity, not as proof that the conjectured replacement actually reproduces apostolic wording. Live burden: he must provide enough passage-specific grounds to show actual loss, or else retain the narrower conclusion that White’s guarantee lacks proof. Locked score: 90/100 because the logical distinction decisively rebuts certainty and conjectural practice supplies relevant evidence, although the example cannot establish widespread primitive loss.

con.words: White clarifies that P75 and Vaticanus belong to a related stream but are not direct parent-child copies, so their agreements reflect distinct transmission within shared ancestry.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White repairs an ambiguity by distinguishing a textual stream from direct parent-child descent and notes that Vaticanus can preserve readings older than P75. Principal limitation: nonidentity and lack of direct copying do not establish that the witnesses independently access the autograph, because related branches may still inherit a common altered ancestor; accordingly the answer improves the manuscript description but cannot make shared-stream agreement equivalent to multiple access routes reaching the original. Live burden: he must characterize their genealogical independence and connect agreements at disputed locations to pre-branch evidence rather than family resemblance alone. Locked score: 83/100 because the clarification answers a simplified objection and preserves corroborative value, yet it does not close Ehrman’s deeper common-ancestor challenge.

pro.words: A hypothetical altered third copy could become the ancestor of every surviving branch, so later agreement and multiplicity would recover that copy rather than the autograph.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman constructs a valid countermodel showing that extensive later branching, agreement, and accurate copying are compatible with an unrecoverable alteration before the surviving genealogy diversified. Principal limitation: the scenario defeats a guarantee but supplies no positive evidence that Philippians, or any identified book, actually passed through such a bottleneck; its disciplined use is therefore to block entailment, leaving historical probability to be assessed from additional manuscript and internal evidence. Live burden: he must keep the inference modal and connect it to concrete early uncertainty if claiming more than the insufficiency of White’s preservation proof. Locked score: 89/100 because the counterexample exposes a central logical vulnerability with exceptional clarity, while remaining hypothetical rather than a historical demonstration.

con.words: White argues that one recognizably continuous New Testament text and theology emerges from early variation, which would be surprising after major primitive corruption.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White appeals to convergence at the level of recognizable books and theology, asking why radically corrupted origins did not generate multiple fundamentally different New Testaments. Principal limitation: one surviving textual tradition can also descend from an early common bottleneck, so later unity does not exclude alterations before diversification or historical loss of competitors; recognizable continuity constrains catastrophic alternatives, but a single successful ancestral form can also generate precisely that later convergence. Live burden: he must show that the observed convergence independently reaches the autograph rather than merely a successful early ancestor. Locked score: 82/100 because continuity is relevant evidence against sweeping corruption, but it answers a stronger claim than Ehrman needs and leaves localized pre-branch changes possible.

pro.words: The Mark variant contrasting Jesus’s anger with compassion changes his depicted emotional response, showing that a single viable word can produce interpretive significance.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman gives an immediately understandable semantic contrast between anger and compassion, demonstrating why counting changed words cannot substitute for evaluating their narrative effect. Principal limitation: this initial presentation does not yet defend which reading is original, and a changed emotion need not transform the entire Gospel or its theology; the emotional opposition establishes semantic consequence independently of any claim that Christian doctrine or Mark’s complete portrait is overturned, preserving interpretive proportionality. Live burden: he must supply internal or external reasons for preferring anger while calibrating the consequence as local characterization. Locked score: 86/100 because the example compellingly establishes meaningful difference, though originality and the magnitude of its wider implication remain unsettled until the later exchange.

con.words: White presses whether the ‘apart from God’ reading can transform Hebrews if Ehrman also argues that the reading fits themes already present elsewhere in the book.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White proportionately tests Ehrman’s book-level language by observing that the preferred ‘apart from God’ reading was defended as consistent with Hebrews, while still allowing a local difference at the verse. Principal limitation: the exchange supplies only a compressed account of the book’s wider theology, so the extent to which this local reading changes Hebrews remains incompletely demonstrated by either speaker; the challenge calibrates consequence rather than erasing the contrast between divine abandonment and divine grace. Live burden: if White extends the challenge beyond calibrating Ehrman’s wording, he must show that the explicit local contrast adds little to the book’s interpretation. Locked score: 88/100 because the question usefully narrows the claimed consequence without denying semantic difference, although the broader textual comparison remains abbreviated.

pro.words: In Hebrews 2:9, ‘apart from God’ portrays unsupported human suffering whereas ‘by the grace of God’ explicitly makes Jesus’s death an act of divine grace.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman articulates the exact interpretive difference between the rival readings and identifies what each would make this passage explicitly teach about Jesus’s death. Principal limitation: his statement that the book’s meaning changes can sound broader than the demonstrated point that one theological proposition becomes explicit or absent at one location; the distinction remains significant even if neither option overturns the book’s entire theology or the broader New Testament message, which preserves necessary interpretive and argumentative proportionality throughout. Live burden: he must distinguish local explicit teaching from compatibility with themes elsewhere in Hebrews and defend the preferred original reading. Locked score: 87/100 because the semantic analysis is concrete and consequential, while its book-level formulation needs tighter calibration and manuscript support.

con.words: White challenges Mark’s anger reading through its isolated support in a free-writing witness and offers contextual harmonization as an alternative explanation for its origin.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White combines external evidence about the unusual witness with a specific internal mechanism by which nearby severe language could prompt a scribe to introduce anger. Principal limitation: describing the manuscript as generally free does not decide this reading, and harmonization remains a competing hypothesis rather than a demonstrated copying event; a convincing resolution requires comparative explanatory power rather than treating either manuscript character or hypothetical scribal motive as independently decisive. Live burden: he must compare the rival directional explanations and show why contextual assimilation outweighs the recognized tendency to soften a difficult portrayal. Locked score: 87/100 because the challenge is passage-specific and evidentially serious, although neither its witness generalization nor proposed mechanism conclusively resolves originality.

pro.words: Ehrman argues that scribes more plausibly softened Jesus’s puzzling anger into compassion, while limiting the result to a fuller nuance within Mark’s characterization.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman supplies a directional internal argument: an awkward angry Jesus gives a scribe an intelligible motive for replacing anger with the easier compassionate reading. Principal limitation: transcriptional plausibility does not independently overcome the sparse external support, and his interpretation still depends on an uncertain judgment about scribal motivation; his later restriction to fuller characterization appropriately prevents the passage-level inference from becoming an exaggerated claim about wholesale theological transformation. Live burden: he must weigh this harder-reading inference against White’s harmonization alternative and the manuscript’s recognized freedom. Locked score: 90/100 because the reply directly explains both textual direction and interpretive consequence with careful calibration, while the external-evidence imbalance prevents decisive certainty.

pro.words: Ehrman distinguishes White’s comparison of reconstructed printed editions from actual manuscript collation and questions whether the reported word agreement generalizes to individual witnesses.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman exposes a crucial denominator distinction between total-word agreement in representative printed texts and percentages used to classify manuscript variation, preventing an impressive number from answering a different empirical question. Principal limitation: White explicitly disclosed that his examples were printed texts, and the exchange does not show the stated edition-level calculation to be inaccurate on its own terms; the methodological distinction narrows extrapolation without discrediting the reproducible comparison that White actually described. Live burden: if Ehrman claims that the statistic misrepresents manuscript reliability, he must demonstrate why transfer from reconstructed editions to individual witnesses fails materially. Locked score: 89/100 because the cross-examination achieves valuable methodological clarification and confines the statistic’s reach, yet leaves the limited printed-text comparison intact.

con.words: Representative Byzantine and critical printed texts agree on more than 95 percent of their total words, indicating extensive continuity between reconstructed textual forms.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White clearly identifies the evidence as printed editions, illustrates the comparison with several passages, and supplies a reproducible total-word measure rather than disguising it as manuscript collation. Principal limitation: representative editorial texts are constructed from traditions and cannot directly quantify pairwise agreement among individual manuscripts or resolve the significance of concentrated differences; its strongest defensible implication is widespread verbal stability between editorial reconstructions, not uniform agreement throughout every surviving handwritten witness. Live burden: he must explain what this edition-level continuity establishes about original wording at meaningful variants. Locked score: 85/100 because the calculation is transparent and relevant to broad continuity, while its inferential reach is narrower than the manuscript-wide reliability conclusion it is asked to support.

pro.words: A small percentage of changed words can reverse or substantially alter meaning, so textual importance must be assessed semantically rather than by word-count proportion.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman’s negation example demonstrates with elementary logic why a one-percent textual difference may reverse an entire sentence, decisively separating frequency from semantic importance. Principal limitation: the hypothetical shows what a strategically placed word can do, not how often extant New Testament variants actually produce comparable effects; the counterexample establishes that magnitude and importance are logically separable, leaving their empirical distribution as a further historical question. Live burden: he must identify meaningful viable cases and calibrate their consequences instead of allowing the illustration to stand for the whole variant population. Locked score: 89/100 because the reasoning defeats percentage-only reassurance and directly motivates passage-level evaluation, although it supplies no prevalence estimate for severe semantic changes.

con.words: White asks whether Ehrman’s uncertainty standard would also undermine quotation of far more sparsely attested classical works, testing whether the New Testament receives consistent treatment.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White introduces a useful comparative standard by noting that classical texts have much longer manuscript gaps yet remain cited and studied through their surviving traditions. Principal limitation: Ehrman accepts the same textual uncertainty for classical works without inferring that historical use is impossible, so the radical-skepticism consequence exceeds his stated position; relative abundance may support higher confidence, but it cannot manufacture certainty that Ehrman never demanded elsewhere. Live burden: if White wants the analogy to resolve meaningful New Testament variants, he must connect general usability to those disputed locations rather than demand certainty about every original word. Locked score: 81/100 because the comparison checks consistency and contextualizes attestation, but its strongest skeptical consequence misses Ehrman’s qualified historical practice.

pro.words: Ehrman applies the same uncertainty to classical literature while maintaining that scholars can responsibly quote manuscript traditions and make graded historical judgments.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman answers the consistency challenge directly, extending his standard to Suetonius and other ancient authors while distinguishing imperfect textual access from wholesale historical ignorance. Principal limitation: the response establishes consistency at a general methodological level but does not itself decide how any particular New Testament variant should be reconstructed; the rebuttal’s proper task is consistency, not a comprehensive confidence schedule for every surviving ancient sentence. Live burden: if he uses the analogy affirmatively for the motion, he must connect graded uncertainty to the selected Jesus sayings; to rebut total skepticism, his consistent practice is sufficient. Locked score: 91/100 because the answer is candid, precise, and directly blocks the alleged collapse of historical knowledge, while appropriately leaving passage-level judgments to their own evidence.

con.words: White secures agreement that scholars still possess sufficiently clear classical texts to quote, arguing that qualified uncertainty can coexist with practical textual knowledge.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White narrows the exchange to an important concession: lack of autographs and residual uncertainty do not prevent responsible quotation from a reconstructed manuscript tradition. Principal limitation: practical usability does not entail certainty at each disputed location, and Ehrman already frames quotation as representing the manuscript tradition rather than pristine originals; the conceded practice supplies an epistemic floor while leaving passage-specific confidence to separate textual analysis. Live burden: if White wants this common ground to defeat the motion, he must connect it to the meaningful Jesus sayings under dispute, without proving every original word. Locked score: 85/100 because the follow-up establishes compatibility between uncertainty and textual knowledge, while supporting general usability more strongly than resolution of specific contested attributions.

pro.words: Ehrman explains that uncertainty about original wording undermined his former expectation that divine inspiration would include accurate preservation, while labeling this a personal argument.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman transparently labels the reasoning personal and poses an intelligible symmetry between divine inspiration of authors and divine preservation through copyists. Principal limitation: the conclusion depends on a contestable theological expectation about what an inspiring deity would choose to preserve, and the argument remains subsidiary to the manuscript evidence bearing directly on the motion; its force therefore turns on theology rather than on additional evidence about copying, genealogy, or surviving readings. Live burden: if this personal expectation is meant to carry independent argumentative weight, he must defend it rather than infer divine intention from textual variation alone. Locked score: 75/100 because the reasoning clearly explains his motivation, but its disputed theological premise and secondary relevance substantially limit its force.

con.words: White argues that apostles freely used nonoriginal-language translations without autograph access, showing that inspiration historically did not require perfectly identical copies for authoritative use.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White tests Ehrman’s preservation expectation against the apostles’ own practice, where authoritative quotation proceeds through translations and textual forms rather than physical originals. Principal limitation: accepting usable translations does not establish that every disputed Jesus saying is recoverable or that no copied wording constitutes local misattribution; the argument’s theological success should therefore remain separate from whether particular later copyists introduced identifiable speech into Gospel narratives. Live burden: White must explain why this precedent sets the relevant preservation standard for the New Testament motion rather than merely rebutting a perfection requirement. Locked score: 90/100 because the counterexample directly and powerfully undermines Ehrman’s theological premise, while leaving the historical textual cases to separate analysis.

pro.words: Ehrman concedes that perfect preservation was not the apostles’ standard, then observes that their Old Testament quotations sometimes reflect textual forms unavailable in present Bibles.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman forthrightly grants that his preservation expectation was not the apostles’ standard and immediately adds a historically relevant qualification: apostolic quotation itself illustrates use of differing textual forms. Principal limitation: the observation confirms textual plurality but does not defend his personal expectation against White’s counterexample, since conceding a different apostolic standard leaves that theological premise independently contested; apostolic variability remains significant independently. Live burden: if he continues to rely on his own expectation, he must explain why it should govern despite apostolic practice; his qualification separately remains relevant to transmission. Locked score: 90/100 because the concession is precise and intellectually responsible, while the added observation preserves a distinct textual point without evading White’s successful challenge.

con.words: White urges textual education and argues that uncontrolled Mediterranean circulation prevented any authority from uniformly altering the message, preparing believers to understand disputed passages without alarm.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White joins a practical educational proposal to his substantive distribution argument, candidly acknowledging famous additions while explaining how widespread circulation constrains centralized manipulation. Principal limitation: education changes audience resilience rather than textual facts, and absence of central control does not eliminate decentralized changes or an alteration before wide dispersion; the pedagogical recommendation is valuable precisely because informed readers can acknowledge textual uncertainty without confusing it with destruction of the entire message. Live burden: he must establish that the circulation pattern preserved the relevant original readings, not merely that later wholesale revision was difficult. Locked score: 82/100 because the recommendation is responsible and the preservation mechanism is relevant, though the closing restates rather than resolves the pre-branch evidential gap.

pro.words: Because Christians historically used whatever manuscripts were available, and all such manuscripts contain mistakes, Ehrman concludes universally that ‘all Bibles misquote Jesus.’
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Ehrman shifts attention from an ideal reconstructed text to the manuscripts historically available to Christian communities, connecting copying mistakes to the Bibles through which readers encountered Jesus’s words. Principal limitation: the universal conclusion that all Bibles misquote Jesus is not established merely by showing that every manuscript contains some mistake, because the premise does not specify whether each manuscript’s errors alter words attributed to Jesus; the inference moves illicitly from universally fallible documents to universal error within the particular quotation category. Live burden: he must supply the missing universal connection or restrict the conclusion to demonstrated manuscripts and passages. Locked score: 86/100 because the historical framing directly addresses actual textual use, but its final quantifier extends beyond the evidence presented for particular Jesus quotations.

con.words: White concludes that textual variants are not misquotations because the manuscript tradition preserves recoverable apostolic teaching and continuity of Jesus’s message despite local differences.
con.critique: Strongest feature: White answers the precise motion explicitly and consistently applies his defended standard: variants are not misquotations when the collective tradition preserves recoverable apostolic teaching and the same message of Jesus. Principal limitation: message-level continuity does not by itself resolve cases where a historical Bible locally presents wording judged nonoriginal, even when the teaching survives elsewhere; the unresolved issue is the adequacy of his definition when textual and message-level answers diverge. Live burden: he must explain why recoverable message is the controlling meaning of misquotation and incorporate the strongest local additions into that account. Locked score: 85/100 because the conclusion is clear, integrated, and stable across his case, while its message standard does not fully answer Ehrman’s local attribution evidence.

strengths: Converted an abstract copying problem into concrete cases involving long additions, disputed sayings, and sharply different readings attributed directly to Jesus.
Repeatedly separated textual percentages from semantic importance and exposed the gap between reconstructing a common ancestor and reaching the lost autograph.
Accepted limited concessions about classical texts, Greek-edition proximity, apostolic standards, and Mark’s local nuance without surrendering the narrower affirmative case.

blunders.text: The personal inspiration argument depended on a contestable theological expectation about divine preservation and remained subsidiary to the manuscript evidence bearing directly on the motion.
The closing claim that all Bibles misquote Jesus was broader than the carefully demonstrated examples and risked obscuring differences in significance and recoverability.

strengths: Corrected the raw-variant denominator by explaining how more manuscripts produce both more differences and more evidence, then classified the genuinely consequential subset.
Developed a substantive preservation model from distributed transmission, tenacity, printed-text continuity, and the absence of centralized control rather than asserting reliability.
Conceded famous textual additions while persuasively distinguishing local proof-text loss from destruction of essential beliefs or the broader apostolic message.

blunders.text: Tenacity and multiple later lines were pressed too close to a guarantee, while White’s convergence reply left Ehrman’s pre-branch bottleneck and conjectural-emendation objections unresolved.
The classical comparison sometimes portrayed Ehrman as requiring radical historical skepticism, although he consistently accepted qualified quotation and probabilistic historical knowledge.

finalArgument.thesis: Actual Bibles can misquote Jesus whenever their presentation attributes wording to him that textual comparison shows was introduced during transmission.
premises: A quotation claim concerns the particular words attributed to a speaker, so preservation of a general message cannot by itself authenticate every local attribution.
The debate establishes substantial passages and individual sayings whose presence in familiar Bibles is not supported as original in the earliest recoverable text.
Distributed manuscripts can reveal later additions, yet agreement among surviving branches cannot logically guarantee that their shared ancestor reproduced the autograph.
Semantic importance depends on what a changed word or passage does, rather than on its fraction of the total manuscript tradition.
Responsible historical knowledge remains possible under graded uncertainty, so acknowledging misquotation at selected locations does not entail global skepticism.
finalArgument.conclusion: Because identifiable transmitted readings place demonstrably secondary wording on Jesus’s lips, while other sayings remain honestly uncertain, the affirmative can prevail locally without denying broad textual recoverability.

newArguments.title: Attribution Risk Asymmetry
newArguments.text: A printed quotation makes a positive attribution: these are the speaker’s words. When a saying is meaningfully disputed, unqualified inclusion assumes more than cautious marking or omission would, so dispute creates a risk of misquotation rather than proving one. The asymmetry matters because message continuity answers whether readers can recover teaching, while quotation marks answer who said particular words. An established secondary reading can ground a misquotation finding; unresolved wording instead warrants visible qualification until the attribution receives stronger support.

newArguments.title: Content Cannot Authenticate Provenance
newArguments.text: A saying may fit Jesus’s familiar teaching perfectly and still lack a defensible transmission path back to him. Contentual harmony shows compatibility, not provenance: a later scribe could compose words that preserve the surrounding message, and doctrinal redundancy would make that composition less conspicuous rather than more authentic. Therefore White’s strongest message-continuity evidence cannot settle the separate historical relation between a particular saying and its alleged speaker. Misquotation can remain local even when the inserted sentence is theologically orthodox and semantically continuous with undisputed material.

finalArgument.thesis: Textual variation does not amount to misquoting Jesus when the collective tradition transparently preserves alternatives and supports recovery of his teaching.
premises: A larger manuscript base necessarily records more copying differences while also providing the comparisons required to detect and correct them.
Most recorded differences are nonmeaningful or nonviable, leaving a much smaller class that can affect interpretation and plausibly be original.
Geographically distributed and uncontrolled circulation makes coordinated replacement of the apostolic message substantially less plausible than localized scribal change.
Even famous secondary passages do not erase essential teachings that remain independently attested in undisputed portions of the text.
Historical quotation routinely rests on critically reconstructed manuscript traditions rather than surviving autographs or certainty about every word.
finalArgument.conclusion: Under White’s defended usage, the Bible does not misquote Jesus because variants remain critically recoverable within a tradition that preserves the same attributable teaching and message.

newArguments.title: Correction Is Publication
newArguments.text: Once a tradition identifies a passage as secondary and marks or brackets it, the published Bible is no longer simply asserting that every displayed line belongs to the original discourse. It is publishing both the received history and the critical judgment needed to interpret it. Misquotation normally involves presenting doubtful words as securely spoken; transparent apparatus changes that communicative act. This does not prove the disputed wording original, but it weakens a universal charge against contemporary Bibles that visibly disclose the uncertainty they transmit.

newArguments.title: Semantic Quotation Fidelity
newArguments.text: Imagine two faithful translations that use different words while expressing the same assertion, implication, and speaker commitment. Calling one a misquotation merely because its wording differs would confuse verbal identity with faithful quotation. The same conceptual distinction can govern textual variants: a local difference counts against quotation fidelity in proportion to the change it makes to the attributed proposition, not merely because another form may be earlier. This principle gives White’s message standard a reasoned foundation while still allowing variants that reverse or materially alter an assertion to remain serious.

noveltyMap.title: Attribution Risk Asymmetry
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Distinguishes the evidential risk created by unresolved attribution from an established misquotation, deriving a requirement for qualification without treating dispute itself as proof of falsity.

noveltyMap.title: Content Cannot Authenticate Provenance
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Separates semantic and doctrinal compatibility from historical provenance, showing why an orthodox, message-consistent addition can still be a local misquotation.

noveltyMap.title: Correction Is Publication
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Adds that brackets and textual notes alter the communicative act of publication by transmitting uncertainty rather than asserting every displayed line as original.

noveltyMap.title: Semantic Quotation Fidelity
noveltyMap.distinctInferentialContribution: Adds a conceptual account of quotation fidelity based on preserved propositions rather than verbal identity, while allowing meaning-changing variants to count against fidelity.
